source_refs.note: Topic 21.4: reactions with NaOH, KCN, ammonia and aqueous silver nitrate, with Quick Check 21.3, printed pages 79-81.

blocks.text: A halogenoalkane reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide to give both substitution and elimination products depending upon the reaction conditions. Hydroxide ion is both a good nucleophile and a good base. So, when it attacks as a nucleophile, it replaces the halogen atom of the halogenoalkane to form a substitution product, alcohol. As a base, it removes both the β-hydrogen atom and the halogen atom to give an elimination product, an alkene. The reaction takes place at higher temperature under reflux conditions to avoid the loss of volatile products. Bromoethane reacts with aqueous sodium hydroxide to give ethanol as well as ethene.

blocks.alt: Displayed bromoethane + NaOH, with 'aqueous' over the arrow, gives displayed ethanol + NaBr.
blocks.caption: Substitution reaction: bromoethane and aqueous sodium hydroxide (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 82).

blocks.alt: Displayed bromoethane + NaOH, with 'alcohol' over the arrow, gives displayed ethene + HOH + NaBr.
blocks.caption: Elimination reaction: bromoethane and sodium hydroxide in alcohol (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 82).

blocks.text: ii. Reactions of Halogenoalkanes with KCN

Since cyanide ion (CN⁻) is a strong nucleophile but a weak base so it reacts with halogenoalkanes to give substitution product, a nitrile. The reaction is typically carried out by heating the halogenoalkane with an ethanolic solution of potassium cyanide under reflux. Bromoethane reacts with potassium cyanide to give propane nitrile.

blocks.alt: Displayed bromoethane + K+ -C(triple bond)N, with 'alcohol' over the arrow, gives displayed propanenitrile, H3C-CH2-C(triple bond)N, + KBr.
blocks.caption: Bromoethane and potassium cyanide (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 82).

blocks.text: iii. Reactions of Halogenoalkanes with Ammonia
Ammonia is a good nucleophile and it reacts with halogenoalkanes a favourably. Different types of amines can be produced if the amounts of halogenoalkane and ammonia are carefully controlled.

blocks.alt: Ammonia, with a lone pair on N, and a curly arrow from N to the carbon of C2H5-Br; a curly arrow from the C-Br bond to Br. The arrow gives ethylamine, H2N-C2H5, + HBr (hydrogen bromide).
blocks.caption: Ammonia and bromoethane (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 82).

blocks.text: Since ethanamine is also a nucleophile, it can compete with ammonia to react with alkyl halide to give diethyl amine.

blocks.alt: Ethanamine (N with C2H5, two H and a lone pair) with curly arrows from N to the carbon of C2H5-Br and from the C-Br bond to Br, giving N-ethylethanamine + HBr (hydrogen bromide).
blocks.caption: Ethanamine and bromoethane (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 83).

blocks.text: N-ethylethanamine will act as a nucleophile and will attack on another bromoethane molecule to form hydrogen bromide.

blocks.alt: N-ethylethanamine (N with two C2H5, one H and a lone pair) with curly arrows from N to the carbon of C2H5-Br and from the C-Br bond to Br, giving N,N-diethylethanamine + HBr (hydrogen bromide).
blocks.caption: N-ethylethanamine and bromoethane (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 83).

blocks.text: If a large excess of bromoethane is used, the reaction may proceed to give quaternary ammonium salt as the final product.

blocks.alt: N,N-diethylethanamine (N with three C2H5 and a lone pair) with curly arrows from N to the carbon of C2H5-Br and from the C-Br bond to Br, giving the quaternary salt: N with four C2H5 groups in square brackets with a positive charge, and Br- outside the brackets.
blocks.caption: N,N-diethylethanamine and bromoethane (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 83).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The printed quaternary salt puts Br- inside the bracket of the positive ion and names it 'N,N,N-triethylethanaminebromide'; it is [(C2H5)4N]+ Br-, N,N,N-triethylethanaminium bromide, as drawn above.
iv. Reactions of Halogenoalkanes with Aqueous Silver Nitrate

This reaction is carried out in a mixture of water and ethanol, the alcohol in this mixture helps to dissolve the halogenoalkane. Water reacts with halogenoalkane as a nucleophile replacing the halide ion.

The released halide ion then reacts with silver nitrate to give a precipitate with a characteristic colour corresponding to the halide ion present. Thus, the reaction helps to detect the halide ion present in halogenoalkanes.

Comparing the rates of formation of silver halides in this reaction gives us a clue about the different reactivities of halides. The quicker the precipitate appears, the more reactive is the halogenoalkane. An iodoalkane produces a precipitate very quicker than bromoalkane. A chloroalkane, however, reacts very slowly.
